attrs.evidence: nest_check.mjs v0.3.0 checkNestBytes: policy resolved, byte-like confirmed, Buffer.from copy, length bound, fatal decode, strict parse, canonical equality -- in that order, with nest-budget-exceeded reached before any decode. cas.mjs v0.3.0 copies every buffer a store returns. nest_bundle.mjs writes nest_bundle.json as canonical octets and nest_bundle.presentation.json for humans. The CLI reads a Buffer and calls checkNestBytes. Gate `gov-nest`.
attrs.statement: AN UNTRUSTED WIRE BOUNDARY BOUNDS THE OCTETS THAT ARRIVED, BEFORE ANYTHING LOOKS AT THEM. The ingress order is: confirm the input is byte-like; COPY it into storage the verifier owns; apply the byte-length bound; decode UTF-8 fatally; parse strictly; canonicalise and require octet equality; only then verify semantics. Bounding a CANONICAL size instead is bounding a number you can only learn by decoding, parsing and re-encoding the thing you were trying not to spend that much work on -- measured, an oversized buffer of invalid UTF-8 reported an ingress refusal rather than a budget refusal, because the decode ran first. AND OWNERSHIP MEANS A COPY. Retaining a caller's buffer, or a buffer an untrusted store handed back, leaves the verifier reasoning about storage somebody else can still write to; law:proof.verifier-input-owned@1 is only literally true when the octets are copied at ingress. THE EXECUTABLE AND THE LIBRARY MUST AGREE: a command-line entry point that parses a file forgivingly and hands the resulting object to an object API has destroyed the evidence the byte boundary exists to check -- measured, a root carrying a duplicate `protocol` member was REFUSED by the byte API and PASSED by the CLI on the same file, which printed a sentence explaining that duplicate names are refused. A proof-wire file IS canonical octets; a human-readable rendering is a separate, separately named artifact that nothing verifies.
